interfaces.name: Sample amplification procedure
interfaces.type_shape: Original existential uniform-TV amplification property. Map may be randomized; no requirement to retain input samples or produce conditionally independent outputs. Randomized-map notation is interpreted by a Markov kernel, not deterministic pushforward alone.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original existential uniform-TV amplification property. Map may be randomized; no requirement to retain input samples or produce conditionally independent outputs. Randomized-map notation is interpreted by a Markov kernel, not deterministic pushforward alone.

members.statement_original:
Let $\mathcal P$ be a class of probability distributions over a domain $\mathcal X$. We say that $\mathcal P$ admits an $(n,n+m,\varepsilon)$ sample amplification procedure if there exists a (possibly randomized) map $T_{\mathcal P,n,m,\varepsilon}:\mathcal X^n\to\mathcal X^{n+m}$ such that
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\|P^{\otimes n}\circ T_{\mathcal P,n,m,\varepsilon}^{-1}-P^{\otimes(n+m)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\varepsilon.\tag{1}
\]

interfaces.name: Minimax error of sample amplification
interfaces.type_shape: Original minimax amplification error: infimum over a single parameter-independent kernel, then supremum over the class. Its infimum need not be attained under the stated generality.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original minimax amplification error: infimum over a single parameter-independent kernel, then supremum over the class. Its infimum need not be attained under the stated generality.

members.statement_original:
For a given distribution class $\mathcal P$ and sample sizes $n$ and $m$, the minimax error of sample amplification is defined as
\[
\varepsilon^\star(\mathcal P,n,m)\triangleq\inf_T\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\|P^{\otimes(n+m)}-P^{\otimes n}\circ T^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{TV}},\tag{4}
\]
where the infimum is over all (possibly randomized) measurable mappings $T:\mathcal X^n\to\mathcal X^{n+m}$.

interfaces.name: Maximum size of sample amplification
interfaces.type_shape: Original maximal additional sample size and small-error abbreviation. Empty/unbounded feasible sets and equality when the infimum is unattained remain unstated conventions.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original maximal additional sample size and small-error abbreviation. Empty/unbounded feasible sets and equality when the infimum is unattained remain unstated conventions.

members.statement_original:
For a given error level $\varepsilon$, the maximum size of sample amplification is the largest $m$ such that there exists an $(n,n+m,\varepsilon)$ sample amplification, i.e.
\[
m^\star(\mathcal P,n,\varepsilon)\triangleq\max\{m\in\mathbb N:\varepsilon^\star(\mathcal P,n,m)\le\varepsilon\}.\tag{5}
\]
For the ease of presentation, we often choose $\varepsilon$ to be a small constant (say $0.1$) and abbreviate the above quantity as $m^\star(\mathcal P,n)$; we remark that all our results work for a generic $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.

interfaces.name: Sufficient statistics
interfaces.type_shape: Original sufficiency definition by both Markov chains. For a nonrandom parameter, the statement requires a parameter-uniform conditional kernel interpretation; regular conditional probability existence is not guaranteed on arbitrary measurable spaces.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original sufficiency definition by both Markov chains. For a nonrandom parameter, the statement requires a parameter-uniform conditional kernel interpretation; regular conditional probability existence is not guaranteed on arbitrary measurable spaces.

members.statement_original: We first recall the definition of sufficient statistics: in a statistical model $\mathcal M=(\mathcal X,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ and $X\sim P_\theta$, a statistic $T=T(X)\in\mathcal T$ is sufficient if and only if both $\theta-X-T$ and $\theta-T-X$ are Markov chains.

interfaces.name: Sample amplification via sufficiency
interfaces.type_shape: Complete general conditional-generation algorithm. Sufficiency makes the kernel independent of the unknown parameter. Values of the kernel at null conditioning events and common versions across parameters remain measure-theoretic requirements.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Complete general conditional-generation algorithm. Sufficiency makes the kernel independent of the unknown parameter. Values of the kernel at null conditioning events and common versions across parameters remain measure-theoretic requirements.

members.statement_original:
1. Input: samples $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, a given transformation $f$ between sufficient statistics
2. Compute the sufficient statistic $T_n=T_n(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$.
3. Apply $f$ to the sufficient statistic and compute $\widehat T_{n+m}=f(T_n)$.
4. Generate $(\widehat X_1,\ldots,\widehat X_{n+m})\sim P_{X^{n+m}\mid T_{n+m}}(\cdot\mid\widehat T_{n+m})$.
5. Output: amplified samples $(\widehat X_1,\ldots,\widehat X_{n+m})$.

interfaces.name: Exponential family
interfaces.type_shape: Original natural exponential-family definition, with full finite-log-partition domain. Openness, Hessian invertibility and boundary differentiation are not added to the original definition.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original natural exponential-family definition, with full finite-log-partition domain. Openness, Hessian invertibility and boundary differentiation are not added to the original definition.

members.statement_original:
The exponential family $(\mathcal X,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ of probability measures is determined by
\[
dP_\theta(x)=\exp(\theta^\top T(x)-A(\theta))\,d\mu(x),
\]
where $\theta\in\Theta$ is the natural parameter with $\Theta=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:A(\theta)<\infty\}$, $T(x)$ is the sufficient statistic, $A(\theta)$ is the log-partition function, and $\mu$ is the base measure.

interfaces.name: Continuity
interfaces.type_shape: Original nonempty-interior and absolutely continuous statistic condition. It is not merely continuity of the parameter map or of the observations.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original nonempty-interior and absolutely continuous statistic condition. It is not merely continuity of the parameter map or of the observations.

members.statement_original: The parameter set $\Theta$ has a non-empty interior. Under each $\theta\in\Theta$, the probability distribution $\mathcal L(T(X))$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

interfaces.name: Moment condition
interfaces.type_shape: Original standardized k-th moment bound uniform in theta. Theorem4.5 uses k=3;4.6 imposes k=10 on each one-dimensional component. A uniform bound across a growing number of components is not expressly quantified.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original standardized k-th moment bound uniform in theta. Theorem4.5 uses k=3;4.6 imposes k=10 on each one-dimensional component. A uniform bound across a growing number of components is not expressly quantified.

members.statement_original:
For a given integer $k>0$, it holds that
\[
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb E_\theta\left[\left\|(\nabla^2A(\theta))^{-1/2}(T(X)-\nabla A(\theta))\right\|_2^k\right]<\infty.
\]
We call it the moment condition $M_k$.

interfaces.name: Sample average
interfaces.type_shape: Original average sufficient statistic and identity-map choice for the exponential-family amplification upper bounds. T_n denotes a statistic as well as its value on a random sample.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original average sufficient statistic and identity-map choice for the exponential-family amplification upper bounds. T_n denotes a statistic as well as its value on a random sample.

members.statement_original:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be i.i.d. samples drawn from $P_\theta$ taking a general form in Definition 4.3, then it is clear that the sample average
\[
T_n(X^n)\triangleq\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nT(X_i)
\]
is a sufficient statistic by the factorization theorem. We will apply the general Algorithm 1 with an identity map between sufficient statistics, i.e. $\widehat T_{n+m}=T_n$.

interfaces.name: Product exponential family
interfaces.type_shape: Original product of one-dimensional exponential families. Keep it separate from the general product distribution class and from Assumptions1/2 imposed componentwise only in4.6.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original product of one-dimensional exponential families. Keep it separate from the general product distribution class and from Assumptions1/2 imposed componentwise only in4.6.

members.statement_original: First, to avoid the unknown dependence on $d$, we additionally assume a product exponential family, i.e. $P_\theta(dx)=\prod_{i=1}^dp_{\theta_i}(dx_i)$, where each $p_{\theta_i}(x_i)$ is a one-dimensional exponential family.

interfaces.name: Estimation error
interfaces.type_shape: Original expected chi-squared minimax estimation risk with estimator-first divergence orientation. Distribution estimators are not required to belong to the model class.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original expected chi-squared minimax estimation risk with estimator-first divergence orientation. Distribution estimators are not required to belong to the model class.

members.statement_original:
For a class of distributions $\mathcal P$ and sample size $n$, the $\chi^2$-estimation error $r_{\chi^2}(\mathcal P,n)$ is defined to be the minimax estimation error under the expected $\chi^2$-divergence:
\[
r_{\chi^2}(\mathcal P,n)\triangleq\inf_{\widehat P_n}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\chi^2(\widehat P_n,P)],
\]
where the infimum is taken over all possible distribution estimators $\widehat P_n$ based on $n$ samples.

interfaces.name: Product structure
interfaces.type_shape: Original unrestricted Cartesian product of coordinate families, with its parameterized notation excerpted from6.4. No exponential-family, continuity or common-parameter restriction is inherent.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original unrestricted Cartesian product of coordinate families, with its parameterized notation excerpted from6.4. No exponential-family, continuity or common-parameter restriction is inherent.

members.statement_original:
When the distribution class $\mathcal P$ has a product structure $\mathcal P=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathcal P_j$, the next theorem shows a better relationship between the amplification error and the learning error.

$P_\theta=\prod_{j=1}^dp_{\theta_j}$ be a product model with $(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)\in\prod_{j=1}^d\Theta_j$.

interfaces.name: Gaussian location model
interfaces.type_shape: Original unknown-mean, known-covariance family. Positive definiteness is not explicitly stated; the exact formula in6.2 needs care for singular covariance.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original unknown-mean, known-covariance family. Positive definiteness is not explicitly stated; the exact formula in6.2 needs care for singular covariance.

members.statement_original: Consider the observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from the Gaussian location model $P_\theta=\mathcal N(\theta,\Sigma)$ with an unknown mean $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ and a known covariance $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$.

interfaces.name: Identity map
interfaces.type_shape: Original Gaussian identity-statistic procedure. Source shorthand says samples drawn from N(0,Sigma) conditioned on their mean; the product sampling convention is supplied by the general algorithm and Example4.2. Do not require the amplified sample to contain the originals.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original Gaussian identity-statistic procedure. Source shorthand says samples drawn from N(0,Sigma) conditioned on their mean; the product sampling convention is supplied by the general algorithm and Example4.2. Do not require the amplified sample to contain the originals.

members.statement_original:
To amplify to $n+m$ samples, note that the sample mean vector is a sufficient statistic here, with
\[
T_n(X_1,\ldots,X_n)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\sim\mathcal N(\theta,\Sigma/n).
\]
Now consider the identity map between sufficient statistics $\widehat T_{n+m}=T_n$ used with algorithm 1. The amplified samples $(\widehat X_1,\ldots,\widehat X_{n+m})$ are drawn from $\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$ conditioned on the event that $T_{n+m}(\widehat X^{n+m})=\widehat T_{n+m}=T_n(X^n)$.

interfaces.name: Linear independence
interfaces.type_shape: Original linear independence modulo zero, not affine independence modulo constants. Assumption1 gives additional nondegeneracy in the theorem; do not silently rewrite Assumption3 as minimality.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original linear independence modulo zero, not affine independence modulo constants. Assumption1 gives additional nondegeneracy in the theorem; do not silently rewrite Assumption3 as minimality.

members.statement_original: The components of sufficient statistic $T(x)$ are linearly independent, i.e. $a^\top T(x)=0$ for $\mu$-almost all $x\in\mathcal X$ implies $a=0$.

interfaces.name: Assumption 4
interfaces.type_shape: Original two-point Hellinger condition for the given sample size n. Its reference to6.4 imports product structure, not that theorem’s two separate TV bounds. It does not require continuity of the full parameter map.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original two-point Hellinger condition for the given sample size n. Its reference to6.4 imports product structure, not that theorem’s two separate TV bounds. It does not require continuity of the full parameter map.

members.statement_original: Let $\mathcal P$ possess the product structure as in Theorem 6.4. For each $j\in[d]$, there exists two points $\theta_{j,+},\theta_{j,-}\in\Theta_j$ such that $1/(10n)\le H^2(p_{\theta_{j,+}},p_{\theta_{j,-}})\le1/(5n)$.

interfaces.name: Discrete distributions
interfaces.type_shape: Original finite alphabet class with one known mass and all other masses unknown. There is no positivity restriction on the other masses.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original finite alphabet class with one known mass and all other masses unknown. There is no positivity restriction on the other masses.

members.statement_original:
Consider the following class $\mathcal P_{d,t}$ of discrete distributions:
\[
\mathcal P_{d,t}=\left\{(p_0,\ldots,p_d):p_i\ge0,\sum_{i=0}^dp_i=1,p_0=t\right\},
\]
where it is the same as the class of all discrete distributions over $d+1$ points, except that the learner has the perfect knowledge of $p_0=t$ for some known $t\in[1/(2\sqrt d),1/2]$.

interfaces.name: Low-rank covariance estimation model
interfaces.type_shape: Original unknown projection-covariance Gaussian model with ambient dimension p and intrinsic dimension d. This is distinct from the known-covariance unknown-mean family of6.2. All nonzero covariance eigenvalues equal1.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Original unknown projection-covariance Gaussian model with ambient dimension p and intrinsic dimension d. This is distinct from the known-covariance unknown-mean family of6.2. All nonzero covariance eigenvalues equal1.

members.statement_original: Consider a low-rank covariance estimation model: $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$, where $\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ could be written as $\Sigma=UU^\top$ with $U\in\mathbb R^{p\times d}$ and $U^\top U=I_d$. In other words, the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ is isotropic on some $d$-dimensional subspace.
